questions.question: What is MASFT's central claim?
options: Multi-agent failures are fundamental design flaws, not LLM limitations to be fixed with better base models
Failures are random noise that averages out once you collect enough production traces
Failures vanish once you swap in a larger, more capable base model for every agent
Failures are caused by transient network outages between agents and their tool APIs
questions.explanation: Berkeley's MASFT categorizes failures as design flaws; they do not disappear by scaling the base model.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the five recurring industry failure modes the lesson lists?
options: Scope creep, where the agent expands the task beyond what the user asked for
Embedding versioning, which the lesson never lists as one of the five modes
Cascading errors, where one wrong call triggers downstream effects across systems
Tool misuse, where the right tool is called with the wrong arguments
questions.explanation: The five are hallucinated actions, scope creep, cascading errors, context loss, tool misuse.

questions.question: What is a cascading error in this lesson?
options: An LLM rate-limit cascade that throttles every downstream tool call for the remainder of that session
A cron scheduling failure that skips the agent's nightly maintenance run entirely without warning
One wrong call triggers downstream effects across systems (a phantom SKU triggers four downstream API calls)
A YAML parser error in the agent's configuration file that blocks the whole startup sequence
questions.explanation: Cascades amplify a single bad call into a multi-system incident; especially severe when agents fake success.

questions.question: Which two manifestations does the LLM Agent Hallucinations Survey list?
options: Hot-token sampling and cold-token suppression during autoregressive decoding
Greedy search collapse and beam-width starvation during response generation
Soft-prompt drift and hard-prompt override during in-context tool selection
Instruction-following Deviation and Long-range Contextual Misuse
questions.explanation: Hallucinations show up as either ignoring system prompt or forgetting/misapplying earlier-turn context.

questions.question: What does success hallucination mean?
options: The agent returns a success message even though the target state did not change (often on a 400 from a tool)
The model reports overconfident scores on public benchmark leaderboards despite weak production accuracy
The user simply assumes the task succeeded when in fact no agent action was ever taken at all
A unit test in the CI pipeline still passes even though the underlying feature is broken
questions.explanation: Re-probe environment state; agents commonly fake completion when they cannot distinguish 'I failed' from 'impossible'.

questions.question: Why is tagging only crashes insufficient?
options: Crashes are slower to detect than content-level regressions in a typical monitoring pipeline
Most agent failures produce valid-looking output that does not crash; content-level checks are needed
Crashes leak PII more often than successful runs that silently return wrong answers
Logging every crash is a paid feature in most observability platforms' pricing tiers
questions.explanation: Crash-based monitoring misses the bulk of agent failures, which are content-shaped.
